_note: The nurse safety suite, Wave 3: a timer on every visit, a panic button that shows the desk where a nurse is for a fixed window, and the desk queue that works both. MyThuso Master Blueprint v4's Engine 4 seed scope ships the 'nurse safety suite from day one', and ThusoIQ Master v3.5 section 58 item 4 names what it must hold: 'check-in/check-out on every visit, panic button and live location to the ops desk'. This file holds the states, the numbers and the refusal sentences; packages/engines/src/safety/domain holds the arithmetic; scripts/emit-field-safety.mjs writes both native copies. Nothing here is a running service. No timer reaches a desk, no panic reaches a person, no position is read from a device, and the nurse-position door in packages/catalog/feeds.json stays shut.
_numbersNote: The four field-safety timings are settings, in settings.items below, in the shape packages/catalog/settings.json gives every setting. Two are decided and two are still proposals. The founder decided the grace and the panic window on 15 September 2026 — "panic 30, grace 60" — and that Operations changes them on the admin rather than in code; each carries decidedBy, decidedOn and why, in the shape packages/catalog/consent.json gives maximumExpiryDecision. The extension steps and ceiling were not part of that decision and keep `decidedBy: null`, which means nobody with the authority to set them has: ThusoIQ Master v3.5's readiness review (58A) marks 'Nurse workforce & field safety' RED, and its next step is to 'approve employment/flex model, caseload, pay, routing, buddy/no-go rules and panic/escort policy'. The build refuses a proposal that loses its `decidedBy` key and a decision that loses who took it or when, so a number cannot quietly become policy by having the question deleted around it.

timer.whyFromTheService: A visit is timed by the service that was booked. A number typed on a screen or sent with a request is a timer that can be set to anything; the duration in the catalogue is the one the patient was quoted and the nurse's day is drawn from.
timer._timingsNote: The grace, the extension steps and the extension ceiling are the settings grace, extension-steps and extension-ceiling below. A timer copies the values in force when it starts and keeps them.

panic._windowNote: How long the desk sees a nurse's position is the setting panic-window below. A panic takes the window in force when it is pressed and keeps its end.
panic.confirmQuestion: Alert the desk that you need help?
panic.whatHappens: The desk is alerted and can see where you are until {ends}. Nobody else can: not the patient, not other nurses, and not any other part of MyThuso.
panic.whatDoesNotHappen: Pressing panic does not call the police or an ambulance. A person at the desk decides that. If you can, call {police} for the police or {ambulance} for an ambulance yourself.
panic._emergencyNumbersNote: {police} and {ambulance} are the numbers in packages/catalog/sos.json, filled in by the domain rules on the web and by scripts/emit-field-safety.mjs for the native apps. An emergency number typed twice is one that can be typed wrong twice.
panic.sharingUntil: The desk can see your position until {ends}.
panic.sharingStopped: The desk stopped seeing your position at {ended}.
panic.pressAgain: If you still need help, press panic again. A new window starts.
panic.sameVisit: A second press by the same nurse for the same visit while its window is open is the same panic, answered again. It is never refused, and a press by anybody else is never folded into it.

simulation.why: How often the simulated feed produces a position while a window is open. It is the simulation's cadence, not a policy: no device reports anything, and the feed is generated on the machine that draws the desk.
simulation.positionRule: The simulated position is the centre of the suburb the nurse works in, at the precision packages/catalog/geography.json declares. It is never the patient's address, because the preview has no address to give.

settings._note: The field-safety timings Operations changes on the admin, in the shape packages/catalog/settings.json gives every setting. The founder decided on 15 September 2026 that Operations sets the grace and the panic window on the admin rather than in code ("Safety: 30min, grace 60min - but configure this on the admin", clarified as "panic 30, grace 60"); the extension steps and ceiling are set in the same place and are still proposals. Each default lives here and nowhere else. What is in force at any moment is these defaults with every accepted admin change replayed in order, kept in the Safety engine's own store through packages/engines/src/settings and, in the web preview, in the tab's memory. Its routes are GET /v1/safety/settings@2 and POST /v1/safety/setting-changes@2, in the shared shape; version one of both carried timings in minutes and nothing else, and is withdrawn. Two of the settings are not timings: who changes the field-safety settings, which only the admin changes and which always names somebody, and which window a phone that read an older one is given, which opens her panic either way.
settings.heading: Field safety settings
settings.intro: How long the desk waits after a visit's booked time before it looks for a nurse, how long it sees her after a panic, and how much longer she may ask for. Operations changes them here, without a code change.

items.label: Grace after the booked time
items.help: How long after a visit's booked duration, and any extensions she took, the desk is told a nurse has not checked out.

default.why: The founder decided on 15 September 2026, "panic 30, grace 60", and that Operations sets it on the admin. The desk is told an hour after a visit's booked duration, and any extensions she took, if the nurse has not checked out. An hour means a visit that runs long for an ordinary reason — a family with questions, a dressing that takes longer than booked — does not page the desk, so a page from the desk still means something. The cost is written here so that it is read: a nurse in trouble who cannot press panic is looked for up to an hour after she should have left. A nurse who can press panic does not wait for the grace at all.

lowest.proposedBecause: The fifteen minutes first proposed on 14 September. Below it the desk is paged for visits that are only running a little over, and a desk paged for nothing learns to ignore the page.

highest.proposedBecause: Twice the founder's hour. Past two hours after her booked time a nurse in trouble who cannot press panic is looked for in the afternoon for a morning visit, and moving it that far is a decision for this contract rather than a setting on a screen.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to visits that start after it. A visit already running keeps the deadline it started with, so a shorter grace never makes a nurse overdue who was not.

guardrail.statement: The desk is always told when a nurse has not checked out, and never later than two hours after she should have left. No value switches the alert off or pushes it past that.

items.label: Panic window
items.help: How long the desk sees a nurse's position after she presses panic.

default.why: The founder decided on 15 September 2026, "panic 30, grace 60", and that Operations sets it on the admin. The desk sees a nurse's position for thirty minutes after she presses panic: enough to pick the panic up, reach her and let a person at the desk decide whether to send somebody, and no longer, because every minute a position is shown is a minute somebody is watching where a nurse is. The window does not stretch: a nurse who still needs help when it ends presses again and a new window starts, which leaves the desk a record of both rather than one share quietly made longer.

lowest.proposedBecause: Shorter than fifteen minutes is shorter than the desk needs to pick a panic up, reach the nurse and send somebody, so the window would end while help was still being arranged.

highest.proposedBecause: The hour first proposed on 14 September. A position shown for longer than that is nearer to tracking a nurse than helping her, and a nurse who still needs help presses again and opens a new window.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to panics pressed after it. A window already open keeps the end it opened with: it is never cut short and never stretched.

guardrail.statement: A panic always shows the desk where the nurse is, and the showing always ends within the hour. No value hides her from the desk or turns a panic into tracking.

items.label: Extension steps
items.help: The extensions a nurse may choose from when a visit runs long.

default.proposedBecause: Three choices a nurse can press with one hand at a door, rather than a number field.

lowest.proposedBecause: A step shorter than five minutes is a snooze rather than an extension, and a snooze is what extension-without-reason exists to refuse.

highest.proposedBecause: The largest step first proposed. One press that adds more than half an hour is a visit being rebooked at the door, which is a conversation for the desk.

lowest.proposedBecause: At least one step, or a nurse whose visit runs long has no way to ask for more time and the desk is paged for a visit that is only running over.

highest.proposedBecause: Three buttons are what a nurse can read and press with one hand at a door. A fourth is a list she has to stop and read.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to visits that start after it. A visit already running keeps the steps it started with.

guardrail.statement: A nurse can always ask for more time, and no single press adds more than half an hour.

items.label: Most a visit may be extended
items.help: The most a visit may be extended in total before only the desk can let it run on.

default.proposedBecause: An hour beyond the booked time is as long as a visit should run before a person at the desk speaks to the nurse, whatever the reason.

lowest.proposedBecause: Half an hour, so that the largest step the range allows can still be taken once.

highest.proposedBecause: Two hours beyond the booked time is as long as a visit should run on a nurse's own word under any setting. Past that a person at the desk speaks to her.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to visits that start after it. A visit already running keeps the ceiling it started with.

guardrail.statement: A visit never runs on a nurse's own word for more than two hours past its booked time.

items.label: A panic from a phone that read an older window
items.help: Whether a panic from a phone that read an older window opens the window in force now, rather than the window the phone sent.

default.proposedBecause: A panic is never refused over bookkeeping, and the window in force is the one Operations decided most recently. Either choice opens the panic: this says only which of two windows the settings have held it opens.

allowed.label: Open the window in force
allowed.proposedBecause: The window Operations set most recently is the one the desk is working to.

allowed.label: Open the window the phone sent
allowed.proposedBecause: The phone told the nurse a window before she pressed, and the window it sent was the policy a moment ago.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to panics pressed after it. A window already open keeps the end it opened with.

items.label: Who changes the field safety settings
items.help: The roles that may change every field-safety setting other than this one.

default.proposedBecause: The founder decided Operations sets the field-safety timings on the admin, and the admin is the role that holds the back office. Until somebody decides otherwise, nobody else changes them.

allowedRoles.proposedBecause: The Control Tower operator works the desk these settings govern and may be asked to hold them. No clinician, nurse or outside party changes how long the desk waits for a nurse.

lowest.proposedBecause: Somebody always answers for the desk's timings. A list of nobody is timings nobody may change, and nobody to ask why they are what they are.

highest.proposedBecause: Both of the roles that may be named.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to the next change anybody makes. A change already made stays made, and the history keeps who made it.

guardrail.statement: Somebody may always change the field safety settings, and nobody but an admin or the Control Tower operator ever may. No value leaves the desk's timings to nobody or hands them to a nurse.

items.label: How long the desk sees an SOS's area
items.help: How long after somebody presses SOS the desk may read the area they chose from the list, before nothing keeps where they were.

default.proposedBecause: Long enough for a nurse offered the visit to accept it, reach the area inside the target the service is sold with and be with the patient, and for the desk to find the area again if the offer is slow to be taken; short enough that the area a frightened person chose is not a record of where they were that afternoon. Standing the SOS down ends it at once, whatever is left.

lowest.proposedBecause: An hour. Shorter, and a nurse accepting a slow offer arrives while the desk can no longer read the area she is going to.

highest.proposedBecause: Four hours. Past that the area is a record of where somebody was rather than help getting to them, which is the tracking a safety feature must not become.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to SOS presses after it. An SOS already pressed keeps the window it was pressed under: a shorter one never hides its area early, and a longer one never keeps it longer.

guardrail.statement: The area an SOS was pressed from is always shared with the desk for a while, and never kept for more than four hours.

items.label: How long next of kin may be tried after an SOS
items.help: How long after somebody presses SOS the desk may still try their next of kin.

default.proposedBecause: Inside the first hour, being told somebody pressed SOS is something a family can still act on: ring them, go round, meet them at a hospital. After it, an attempt reads as news of something that may already be over, and a family rung about it is frightened without being helped.

lowest.proposedBecause: A quarter of an hour is as short as the desk can pick an SOS up, see that next of kin were not told and try again.

highest.proposedBecause: Three hours. Past that the desk speaks to the family as a person would, rather than a retry going out about a press that long ago.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to SOS presses after it. An SOS already pressed keeps the window it was pressed under.

guardrail.statement: Next of kin can always be tried soon after an SOS, and are never tried more than three hours after it.

items.label: How many more times next of kin may be tried
items.help: After the attempt recorded when somebody presses SOS, how many more times the desk may try their next of kin about that SOS.

default.proposedBecause: Two more tries lets the desk try again when a phone was off or out of signal, without a family's phone ringing again and again about one press. Nought is allowed: it means they are tried once, when SOS is pressed.

lowest.proposedBecause: Nought more tries still tries them once, when SOS is pressed, so no value leaves next of kin untried.

highest.proposedBecause: Five more tries inside the window is already a family's phone ringing every few minutes. Past that the desk rings them itself, which is a conversation rather than a retry.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to SOS presses after it. An SOS already pressed keeps the number of tries it was pressed under.

guardrail.statement: Next of kin are tried at least once when somebody presses SOS, and never more than six times about one SOS.

items.label: Sentinel baseline window
items.help: How many days back does a patient's Sentinel baseline count readings with clinical weight from?

default.proposedBecause: A month: long enough to hold several visits' readings for a patient seen weekly, short enough that a baseline describes the patient as they are now. Nobody clinical has decided it, and it decides nothing about whether a reading is concerning, because no baseline rule is ratified.

lowest.proposedBecause: A week. Fewer days than that and a patient seen weekly has one reading in their baseline.

highest.proposedBecause: Six months. Longer than that and a baseline describes somebody the patient may have stopped being.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to baselines opened after it. A baseline already open keeps the window and the settings version it was opened under.

guardrail.statement: A Sentinel baseline always looks back at least a week, and never more than six months.

items.label: Readings before a Sentinel baseline is formed
items.help: How many readings with clinical weight must a patient's baseline hold inside its window before it is shown as formed?

default.proposedBecause: Five readings is about a month of weekly visits, enough that one unusual day is one reading among several. A formed baseline is a count and nothing more: no baseline rule is ratified, so nothing is worked out from it.

lowest.proposedBecause: Fewer than three and a single reading is a third of the baseline.

highest.proposedBecause: Thirty is a reading a day for a month. Asking for more leaves most patients' baselines forming for good.

items.appliesTo: A change applies to baselines opened after it. A baseline already open keeps the minimum and the settings version it was opened under.

guardrail.statement: A Sentinel baseline is never shown as formed from fewer than three readings, and never asks for more than thirty.

items.label: Nurses working a suburb before a proportion of them may be drawn
items.help: How many nurses must be rostered to a suburb before the dispatch map may draw the proportion of them with something open. Below it the map draws the counts and says why it draws no proportion.

default.proposedBecause: Five is the smallest group a proportion can be drawn over without naming somebody. This is k-anonymity rather than a matter of taste: the roster has nine nurses across six suburbs — Soweto three, Randburg two, and Tembisa, Rosebank, Melville and Alexandra one each — so in Soweto a proportion of one third is one of three named people, and in Melville a proportion is one person described as a percentage of herself. A figure like that is not an aggregate at all; it is a nurse's afternoon with the serial numbers filed off, and it lands on a map a controller reads while deciding where to send the next visit. Five is also the number below which the count itself is already the whole answer, so nothing is lost by drawing the count instead. Nobody has decided it; it is a proposal until Operations sets it.

lowest.proposedBecause: Three is the floor beneath which the word proportion stops being true of anything: with two nurses a proportion is one of two people, and with one it is a single nurse's afternoon drawn as a statistic. No value below three may be set, so no setting can turn this overlay into a way of naming an individual on a map.

highest.proposedBecause: Twenty nurses in one suburb is beyond anything this roster could field — its largest suburb holds three — so a floor that high suppresses every proportion on the board and leaves the counts alone, which is what a floor of twenty would honestly mean. It is allowed as a way of drawing no proportion anywhere, but it should be set by somebody saying that out loud rather than reached by drift.

items.appliesTo: A change applies the next time the overlay is drawn. Nothing is kept between draws, so there is no earlier proportion to preserve and no live figure that could be changed under a reader.

guardrail.statement: No proportion is ever drawn over fewer than three nurses, and the count of open items is drawn whatever this is set to.

changelog.by: Safety lead (Wave 3), proposed and not decided
changelog.why: The first proposals, so the nurse's strip and the desk could be built and tested against something.
"Safety: 30min, grace 60min - but configure this on the admin", clarified as "panic 30, grace 60". The extension steps and ceiling were not part of the decision and stay proposals.

changelog.by: Platform Settings lead (Wave 3), proposed and not decided
changelog.why: Two answers that lived in code became settings when the founder instructed that open questions be admin settings: who may change the field-safety settings, and which window a phone that read an older one is given.

changelog.by: Safety lead (Wave 4), proposed and not decided
changelog.why: Patient SOS and next of kin came onto the engine. How long the desk sees the area an SOS was pressed from, how long next of kin may be tried after it and how many more times are open questions nobody has decided, so they are settings with proposed defaults, under the founder's instruction that open questions become admin settings.

changelog.by: Safety lead (Wave 5), proposed and not decided
changelog.why: Sentinel's baselines came onto the engine. How far back a baseline counts and how many readings it needs before it is shown as formed are open questions nobody clinical has decided, so they are settings with proposed defaults that wait on a clinical review, under the founder's instruction that open questions become admin settings.

changelog.by: Safety lead (Wave 6), proposed and not decided
changelog.why: The dispatch map's field-safety overlay came onto the engine: what is open in each suburb right now, drawn on the zones a controller already dispatches against. The count of open items needs no setting and has none — it is the desk queue's own rows grouped by suburb, drawn whole, because an open panic in a suburb with one nurse on the roster is exactly the incident the operator most needs to see and a floor that hid it would be a safety feature protecting a suburb's reputation instead of a person. What needed a number is the one figure on that overlay with a denominator, the proportion of a suburb's nurses with something open, because a proportion makes a claim about a place and that claim has to be over a group large enough not to be a claim about a person. How large is an open question nobody has decided, so it is a setting with a proposed default under the founder's instruction that open questions become admin settings. It waits on no clinical review: nothing about it is clinical, and it decides nothing about a patient. What it does sit beside is geography.json's no-history-drawn and this contract's own nothing-is-kept — the overlay draws no score, no trend and no ranking, because a ranking of suburbs would need a record of what happened in each, and there is no reviewer in this repository qualified to make the call a score would make about whether a patient is seen at home or on a screen.

timer.label: On a visit
timer.means: The timer is counting down to when she should have checked out.

timer.label: Past check-out
timer.means: The time plus the grace has passed and she has neither checked out nor extended.

timer.label: Checked out
timer.means: She checked out, or the visit was completed and signed.

panic.label: Waiting for the desk
panic.means: Pressed, and nobody at the desk has picked it up.

panic.label: The desk has it
panic.means: A person at the desk has picked it up.

panic.label: Resolved
panic.means: The desk recorded what happened. Sharing has stopped.

extensionReasons.label: The visit is taking longer than booked
Waiting for the patient or the family
Waiting for a doctor to call back

checkInRule.statement: Saying you are safe is recorded and the desk sees it. It never moves when you should check out, and it never closes what the desk was told: a person at the desk does that.
checkInRule.whyNoDeadline: An I am safe that moved the deadline, pressed every quarter of an hour, would be an extension with no reason and no ceiling: the exact thing an extension refuses.
checkInRule.whyTheDeskCloses: The desk was the one paged. Her word that she is safe is shown beside the overdue it answers, and the reason the nurse-answered close is true, but a person who saw the page closes it. The conservative choice, taken on 15 September 2026 by the Safety lead: a phone that could stand the desk down is a phone that could be made to by whoever is holding it.

_extensionReasonsNote: A reason is what the desk reads beside an extended timer, so none of them says anything about the patient's health. 'Waiting for a doctor to call back' names who, never why.

silenceReasons.label: I reached the nurse by phone and she is safe
The nurse checked in, extended or checked out herself
A colleague confirmed she is safe

outcomes.label: Safe after the desk spoke to her
A person at the desk called the police or an ambulance
Pressed by mistake, confirmed with the nurse

nurse.heading: Your safety
nurse.left: {minutes} min left. If you have not checked out by then, the desk is told.
nurse.overdue: Past check-out since {since}. The desk has been told.
nurse.answered: You said you were safe at {at}.
nurse.saidSafe: You said you were safe at {at}. Your check-out time has not moved.
nurse.closedBySigning: Checked out when the visit was signed at {at}.
nurse.extendQuestion: Why do you need more time?
nurse.extendLeft: Up to {minutes} more minutes can be added to this visit.

desk.heading: Nurses in the field
desk.empty: No nurse is past check-out and nobody has pressed panic. The queue fills itself; there is nothing to refresh.
desk.waiting: {waiting} waiting to be picked up · {open} open
desk.reasonQuestion: Why is it safe to close?

neverCarries.why: What the visit was for is clinical. A queue of 'Family planning' and 'Mental-health check-in' rows is a disclosure to everybody standing behind the desk.
The desk needs to know which nurse and which suburb. The patient's name is in the visit, for the nurse, not on a board.
geography.json's address-is-not-a-pin, read at the desk: a suburb is enough to send somebody, and the nurse's position is shown during a panic and nowhere else.

desk.order: A panic nobody has picked up, then a timer nobody has picked up, then everything the desk already has. Oldest first inside each.

_zoneOverlayNote: The dispatch map's field-safety overlay: what is open in each suburb right now, drawn on the zones a controller is already dispatching against. It exists because the desk queue and the dispatch board are two pictures of one afternoon — an operator choosing which nurse to send to Soweto while a panic is open in Soweto was reading two screens and reconciling them by hand. It is a grouping of GET /v1/safety/desk-queue@1's own rows by suburb, and nothing else: no route of its own, no store, no figure that outlives the render that drew it.

zoneOverlay.heading: Field safety by suburb
zoneOverlay.countsOf: open panics and overdue nurses, in each suburb, now
zoneOverlay.noZoneSentence: No nurse is past check-out and nobody has pressed panic anywhere on this board.
zoneOverlay._listNotAColourNote: The overlay is a list of suburbs with their counts, drawn beside the map, and it is never a colour on the map's zone circles. a-zone-is-not-a-verdict below is the reason: a shaded suburb is a grade whatever the legend says, and a controller reads a red circle as a verdict on a place before she reads the words beside it. Naming the suburb and the count is also what lets the list hold a suburb the map has no circle for — Tembisa and Alexandra are on the roster and are not zones in geography.json, so a nurse overdue in either would be missing from a colouring and present in a list. The list is the honest one, and it costs the patient's first view nothing: it is drawn from features/Dispatch.tsx, in the staff chunk, and touches neither LiveMap nor geography.json.
zoneOverlay.whyCountsAreNeverFloored: The floor below governs the proportion and never the counts. An open panic in a suburb with one nurse on the roster is exactly the incident the operator most needs to see, and a suppression rule that hid it would be a safety feature protecting a suburb's reputation instead of a person. The counts are drawn whole, and they are the operator's own desk queue grouped by suburb, which she is already entitled to read row by row. The floor's job is the different one of stopping three data points becoming a characterisation of a place.

share.label: Proportion of nurses with something open
share.help: The open items in a suburb as a proportion of the nurses rostered to it. It is the only figure on this overlay with a denominator, and the only one the floor governs.
share.suppressedSentence: {rostered} nurse{nursePlural} — too few to draw a proportion over
share.whyADenominator: A count of open items is a fact about this afternoon. A proportion is a claim about a place, and a claim about a place needs a group large enough that it is not a claim about a person: one of nine nurses with something open and one of one nurse with something open are the same count and very different statements, and the second is a woman's afternoon drawn as a statistic. The floor below is k-anonymity, and it governs the proportion alone — the counts are drawn whole whatever it is set to.
share._whyTheSuppressedSentenceIsShortNote: It is drawn once per suburb on a board whose ordinary state is four suburbs with one nurse each, so it is repeated four times a draw. It says the roster size and that it is too few, and the floor's own number and reasoning sit once in the note under the list rather than in every row. A sentence repeated per row that carried the whole argument would be a wall of text an operator stops reading, and the argument read once is the one that lands.

drawnFor.statement: Only the audience that route admits — the operator — sees open panics and overdue nurses on the dispatch map. The board is rendered in three places: the Control Tower's own workspace, the back office's Operations tab, and the merged portal, whose audience is whoever opened it. The back office is not a caller of the desk queue and never gets the overlay; the portal gets it when and only when its audience is the Control Tower, which is the same condition the portal's own field alert already draws the queue under.
drawnFor.elseSentence: The field-safety overlay is not drawn here. It is a grouping of the desk queue, and the desk queue is the operator's.

rules.statement: This overlay computes no score, no rate over time, no trend and no ranking of suburbs. It counts what is open now, and draws a proportion of a suburb's nurses where the roster is large enough for one to be an aggregate.
rules.why: geography.json's no-history-drawn says no map here draws where anybody has been, and a score is that rule broken with arithmetic instead of pixels: to rank a suburb you must keep what happened in it, and keeping it is the tracking the whole safety suite is arranged against. There is also no reviewer for the claim a score would make. A number on a map that says a suburb is dangerous decides whether a patient is seen at home or on a screen, and nothing in this repository is qualified to make that call — ThusoIQ Master v3.5's readiness review marks nurse field safety RED and its next step names a buddy/no-go policy that does not exist.

rules.statement: The counts are worked out from the live desk queue every time the overlay is drawn and are never stored, cached or compared with an earlier draw. A suburb has no field-safety record.
rules.why: A figure that survives its render becomes a history whatever it was called, and the first version of this overlay that remembered yesterday's count would be the product's first record of where trouble had been. Deriving it from the queue is also what stops it disagreeing: the queue is the arithmetic on the timers and panics, so the map cannot say two are open while the desk says one.

rules.statement: No sentence here names a suburb as safe or unsafe, and no colour on this overlay is a grade. A suburb with something open is drawn as a suburb with something open.
rules.why: The words on a screen are what an operator repeats. 'Soweto is high risk' is a claim about a place and about the people in it, made by a count of three; 'two nurses are past check-out in Soweto' is a thing she can act on in the next minute. The second sentence is also the only one this product has the data for.

zoneOverlay._carriesNote: `rostered` is the denominator — how many nurses work the suburb, from packages/catalog/roster.json — and it is a count of people, never a person. It is named `rostered` rather than `nurses` on purpose: neverCarries below names the field `nurse`, and a substring check on the two would collide with the one word that is a count of them. The collision avoided is the point of the awkward name.

neverCarries.why: The overlay says how many, in which suburb, and never who. Who is on the desk queue's own rows, where the operator picks an item up; a map that named a nurse would be a second copy of the queue with a person's name pinned to a suburb.

A zone's counts are drawn on the zone's own centre, from geography.json, which the board already draws. A panic's position is shown on its own row while its window is open and nowhere else — panics.ts drops the coordinate when sharing ends, and this overlay reads the queue, not the position.

The desk queue never carries one and neither does a grouping of it: what a visit was for is clinical, and a map reading 'two family-planning panics in Soweto' discloses it to everybody standing behind the desk.
no-zone-risk-score above. There is no score to carry.
nothing-is-kept above. Nothing is remembered from an earlier draw, so there is no history to carry.

refusals.statement: A visit whose code did not match has not started, so it has no timer.
refusals.why: appointment.in_progress carries visitCodeMatched so that a subscriber can refuse one that says otherwise.

refusals.statement: That visit's service is not in the catalogue, so there is nothing to time it by.
refusals.why: A timer with a guessed duration is a timer that fires at the wrong time.

refusals.statement: This position is no longer shared. Sharing ended at {ended}.
refusals.why: The window always ends, and the desk is told when rather than shown the last place she was. The route's own refusal, position-no-longer-shared, says the same without the time, because a route's sentence has no token to fill.

refusals.statement: The window does not stretch. A nurse who still needs help presses panic again.
refusals.why: A share that can be extended from the desk is a share with no end.

refusals.statement: A position is gone when sharing stops. Nothing keeps where she was.
refusals.why: geography.json's no-history-drawn: a safety feature that keeps positions is a tracking system.

_routeRefusalsNote: Refusals that already belong to a route are named by route, at its version, and id and read from packages/catalog/apis/safety.json, so the sentence the API returns and the sentence a screen shows are one string. A route answered at more than one version names the version, because extend and close were versioned on 15 September and the withdrawn version one keeps the sentences it was frozen with. The desk's and the nurse's refusals moved there from this file on the same day, when their routes were declared; a sentence in both places is two sentences that can disagree. The settings routes' refusals are packages/catalog/settings.json's, shared by every engine, and are read from there.
_engineRefusalsNote: Refusals more than one route answers, declared once for the engine in packages/catalog/apis/safety.json with the routes that answer them in answeredBy, and read from there.
